newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech crown pips mark but trade gap jitters loom.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown pips mark but trade gap jitters loom.

text.p: Uncertainty over the Czech budget and trade deficits have put the Prague foreign exchange market on edge again, as the crown firmed against the mark on Tuesday although it was expected to ease later in the week.
The crown moved to 18.30 to the mark from 18.60 on Tuesday, mainly on the back of the dollar's gains versus the mark which the crown shadows.
"Mark/Czech (crown) is copying the dollar/mark movements," said Petr Korous at Ceskoslovenska Obchodni Banka.
Hence the crown lost ground against the firming U.S. currency to about 34.250 midday from Monday's 34.000 level.

"The mainstream opinion is the crown should lose ground... not in some massive jump, I don't see any massive attacks right now. For the next days I expect 18.60 to 18.85 (against the mark)," Korous said.
But dealers said market jitters should grow ahead of Friday's release of July foreign trade results. The uncertainty is expected to drive the crown lower later in the week.

"Basically we are waiting to see what was the impact of the floods (on trade figures). It's really hard to say, because I doubt there is any reasonable prediction about this figure," said Breta Tichanek at ING Bank.
"Most of the people are sitting on their positions and waiting, most of them are expecting to see the crown weaker."
The impact of recent floods and the spring depreciation in the currency have made forecasts difficult and crown positions more risky.
Early forecasts say the July trade figures would show a deficit of between 10 to 12 billion crowns ($290 to $350 million) after it fell to 9.58 billion crowns in June from 11 billion in May.

"All the banks say the trade figures will be disastrous, but I don't think the figures will have any huge impact on trading because if these figures are worse people will say 'ah, it's just the floods'," Korous said.

Analysts have widely predicted another medium-to-long-term drop in the crown to between 19 to 22 to the mark after a sharp drop in the spring when speculators attacked the currency amid weak macroeconomic results and political instability.

The renewed worries stem from the July floods in the east of the country and their effect on the trade balance and the state budget, and an expected fight within the ruling coalition over next year's budget.
The 1997 budget is forecast to show a deficit of up to 20 billion crowns, despite 45.5 billion in spring spending cuts aimed at balancing the impact of the crown's depreciation.

Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said on Monday that it would be impossible to balance the budget and that the deficit could reach as high as 20 billion crowns, even with planned temporary tax hikes to offset flood relief costs.

"This is a kind of unexpected news, it's negative, and this makes me feel the crown would lose some more ground, but it's difficult to predict what will be the scope of the movement because dollar/mark is complicating that," Korous said.
